'''Arnold Ephraim Ross''' (August 24, 1906 – September 25, 2002) was a [[mathematician]] and [[Mathematics education|educator]] who founded the Ross Mathematics Program, a [[number theory]] summer program for [[Gifted education|gifted]] [[High school (United States)|high school]] students. He was born in Chicago, but spent his youth in [[Odesa]], Ukraine, where he studied with [[Samuil Shatunovsky]]. Ross returned to Chicago and enrolled in [[University of Chicago]] graduate coursework under [[E. H. Moore]], despite his lack of formal academic training. He received his Ph.D. and married his wife, Bee, in 1931.

Ross taught at several institutions including [[Saint Louis University (United States)|St. Louis University]] before becoming chair of [[University of Notre Dame]]'s mathematics department in 1946. He started a teacher training program in mathematics that evolved into the [[Ross Mathematics Program]] in 1957 with the addition of high school students. The program moved with him to [[Ohio State University]] when he became their department chair in 1963. Though forced to retire in 1976, Ross ran the summer program until 2000. He had worked with over 2,000 students during more than forty summers.

The program is known as Ross's most significant work. Its attendees have since continued on to prominent research positions across the sciences. His program inspired several offshoots and was recognized by mathematicians as highly influential. Ross has received an [[honorary doctorate]] and several professional association awards for his instruction and service.

== Early life and career ==

[[File:Arnold Ross as young boy in school uniform.jpg|thumb|left|Ross as young boy in school uniform]] Ross was born Arnold Ephraim Chaimovich<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> on August 24, 1906, in [[Chicago]] to Ukrainian-Jewish immigrants.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> He was an only child.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> His mother supported the family as a physical therapist.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Ross returned to [[Odesa]], Ukraine with his mother in 1909 for assistance from her extended family,<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> and stayed once [[World War I]] and the [[Russian Revolution]] broke out.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> The two events led to widespread famine and economic woe in the region.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Ross learned Russian at the behest of his mother, and developed a love of the theater and language.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Ross's mother encouraged him to read, which he did often, and subscribed to a private library since Odesa had no public library.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> He credited his favorite uncle, an X-ray diagnostician, with introducing him to mathematics.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> The uncle had hired [[Samuil Shatunovsky]] to tutor his talented son, and Ross asked to join in.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> As money meant little due to inflation, Shatunovsky was paid to tutor the two boys with a pound of French hard candy.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> During this time, Ross was not taught with textbooks or lectured on geometric proofs.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> His geometry teacher would ask the class to prove and justify ideas on the blackboard per trial and error.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Many universities were closed due to the famine, but [[Odesa University]] reopened and let a small group of adolescents attend, including Ross.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/>

[[File:Arnold Chaimovich as a young man in Odessa, around 1922 (?).jpg|thumb|right|Ross in Odesa circa 1922]] Ross left Odesa—now part of Ukraine—in 1922 with the intention of returning to Chicago and studying [[topology]] with [[E. H. Moore]] at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> After negotiating his way home, he worked at a family friend's bookbinding shop and continued to learn English at the [[Lewis Institute]].<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> He also changed his surname from Chaimovich to Ross in 1922.<ref name="NAMS 2003"/> Ross used his salary from a year at the shop to enroll for one term at the University of Chicago in Moore's course.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Moore gave Ross special attention, knowing his untraditional background, and arranged for Ross to attend the topology class as the sole undergraduate.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/>

In Moore's teaching style, he would propose a conjecture and task the students with proving it.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Students could respond with counter-conjectures that they would defend.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Ross found Moore's method exciting,<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> and his pedagogy influenced Ross's own.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> Ross graduated with a B.S. degree<ref name="AMM 1986"/> and continued his study as [[Leonard Eugene Dickson]]'s research assistant.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> Ross earned a M.S. degree<ref name="AMM 1986"/> and finished his Ph.D. in number theory at the University of Chicago in 1931 with Dickson as his adviser.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> Ross's dissertation was entitled "On Representation of Integers by Indefinite Ternary Quadratic Forms".<ref name="NAMS 2001"/>  He did not pay tuition after his first quarter, which he credits to Dickson.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/>

Ross married Bertha (Bee) Halley Horecker, a singer-musician and daughter of Ross's Chicago neighbors, in 1931,<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> received a [[United States National Research Council|National Research Council]] Fellowship for 1932,<ref name="RNAS"/> and worked as a [[United States National Research Council|National Research Council]] postdoctoral fellow<ref name="AMM 1986"/> at [[California Institute of Technology]] with [[Eric Temple Bell]] until 1933.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> Ross moved back to Chicago and led the mathematics department at an experimental school started by Ph.D.s during the [[Great Depression]], People's Junior College,<ref name="AMM 1986"/> where he also taught physics.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Ross became an assistant professor at [[Saint Louis University (United States)|St. Louis University]] in 1935 and stayed for about 11 years.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> In an interview, he said he advocated for a student who became the first black woman in [[Southern United States|the South]] to receive a [[master's degree]] in mathematics.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> This exception led the university to admit black students despite the idea's widespread unpopularity.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> During [[World War II]], Ross served as a research mathematician for the [[U.S. Navy]].<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> He befriended Hungarian mathematician [[Gábor Szegő]] while in [[St. Louis]], who recommended Ross for a 1941 [[Brown University]] summer school that prepared young scientists to assist in the war, a program Ross attended.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> He occasionally worked on [[proximity fuzes]] for [[Stromberg-Carlson]]'s laboratory from 1941 to 1945<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> before accepting a position as head of [[University of Notre Dame]]'s mathematics department in 1946.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> He set out to change the school's research climate by inviting distinguished mathematicians including [[Paul Erdős]], whom Ross made a full professor.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/>

== Ross Mathematics Program ==

While at Notre Dame in 1947, Ross began a mathematics program that prioritized what he described as "the act of personal discovery through observation and experimentation" for high school and junior college teachers.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> In 1957, the program expanded via the [[National Science Foundation]]'s post-[[Sputnik]] funds for teacher retraining, and Ross let high school students attend.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> This expansion became the Ross Mathematics Program,<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> a summer mathematics program for talented high school students.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> The program lasts eight weeks and brings students with no prior knowledge to topics such as [[Gaussian integers]] and [[quadratic reciprocity]].<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> Though the program teaches number theory, by its Gauss-inspired<ref name="Bauldry 2011"/> motto, "Think deeply of simple things," its primary goal is to offer precollege students an intellectual experience<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> as what he described as "a vivid apprenticeship to a life of exploration."<ref name="NAMS 2001"/><ref name="NAMS 1998"/> The program is known for its intensity, and is considered America's "most rigorous number theory program."<ref name="Wissner-Gross 2007"/> Ross was known to say, "No one leaves the program unchanged."<ref name="MAA FOCUS 2003"/>

{{Quote box |quote=This emphasis on computation alone too often produces students who have never practiced thinking for themselves, who have never asked why things work the way they do, who are not prepared to lead the way to future scientific innovation. It is precisely this independence of thought and questioning attitude that the Ross Program strives to nurture. |source=Ross Program brochure<ref name="Wissner-Gross 2007"/> |quoted=1 |align=right |width=300px }}

The program usually has 40–50 first-year students, 15 junior counselors, and 15 counselors.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> Students are admitted by application—which includes a set of mathematical questions—or by showing "a great eagerness to learn."<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> First-year students meet daily for lectures in elementary number theory and thrice weekly for problem seminars.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> They are encouraged to think like scientists and devise their own proofs and conjectures to the problems posed,<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> which occupies most of their free time.<ref name="Wissner-Gross 2007"/> Ross designed the daily [[problem set]]s,<ref name="MAA FOCUS 2003"/> and many questions contain his signature directions: "Prove or disprove and salvage if possible."<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Successful students are asked to return as junior counselors and counselors in future summers.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> Junior counselors revisit the daily lectures and help first-years with their questions.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> They also can take advanced courses such as [[combinatorics]]<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> and graduate seminars.<ref name="MAA FOCUS 2003"/> Student problem sets are graded daily by the live-in counselors.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/>

The program was funded in the 1960s by a [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF) program that supported summer programs in science education, but not returning students.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> As NSF support fluctuates, the program has been funded by various means including gifts from donors, scholarships from businesses, a [[National Security Agency]] grant, the university, and its mathematics department.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> It also receives financial support from the [[Clay Mathematics Institute]].<ref name="NAMS 2001"/><ref name="Wissner-Gross 2007"/>

The program grew rapidly with input from prominent mathematicians such as [[Ram Prakash Bambah]], [[Hans Zassenhaus]], [[Thoralf Skolem]], and [[Max Dehn]].<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> In the 1960s and 1970s, Ross brought mathematicians including Zassenhaus, [[Kurt Mahler]], and [[Dijen K. Ray-Chaudhuri]] to teach there regularly.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Ross left Notre Dame to become chair of [[Ohio State University]]'s mathematics department in 1963, and the program followed in the 1964 summer.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/>  The program briefly moved to the University of Chicago in the summers of 1975–1978 at mathematician [[Felix Browder]]'s invitation.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> The program is unadvertised and depends on personal contacts and word of mouth to propagate.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/><ref name="NAMS 1996"/><ref name="Wissner-Gross 2007"/> It is recognized by mathematicians as one of the best mathematics programs for high school students.<ref name="Wissner-Gross 2007"/>

Admission to the program is competitive, with an approximately 15% acceptance rate.<ref>{{cite web |title=Frequently Asked Questions |url=https://rossprogram.org/students/faq/ |website=The Ross Mathematics Program |access-date=22 October 2023}}</ref>

== Retirement and death ==

Ross reached his mandatory retirement from Ohio State University in 1976,<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> when he became Professor Emeritus,<ref name="AMM 1986"/> but continued to run the summer program through 2000,<ref name="MAA FOCUS 2003"/> after which he had a stroke that left him physically impaired and unable to teach.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Daniel Shapiro led the program upon Ross's exit.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/><ref name="Edgar 2007"/> Shapiro was a former counselor at the program.<ref name="NAMS 2003"/>

Ross received an [[honorary doctorate]] from [[Denison University]] in 1984,<ref name="AMM 1986"/> the 1985 [[Mathematics Association of America]] (MAA) Award for Distinguished Service,<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> the 1998 MAA Citation for Public Service,<ref name="NAMS 1998"/> and was named an [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] Fellow in 1988.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> His teaching awards include Ohio State's Distinguished Teaching and Service Awards, and membership on the [[National Science Foundation]]'s science education advisory board.<ref name="AMM 1986"/>

Ross helped begin similar programs in [[West Germany]], India, and Australia.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/> He consulted for an Indian gifted children program in 1973, assisted in an [[Australian National University]] January summer program for talented youth based on Ross's own from 1975 to 1983, and helped start another program in [[Heidelberg]], Germany in 1978.<ref name="AMM 1986"/> He had previously created other mathematics programs, including the teacher training program (before it included high school students)<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> and another program for [[Columbus, Ohio]] [[inner city]] middle and high school students called "Horizons Unlimited" in 1970.<ref name="AMM 1986"/>

Ross's wife, Bee, died in 1983 and left Ross in a deep depression.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> His colleagues said he "lived only for his summer program" in this period.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> He later met a French widow of a diplomat, Madeleine Green, and they married in 1990.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/>

Ross died on September 25, 2002.<ref name="MAA FOCUS 2002"/> ''[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]'' and ''[[MAA FOCUS]]'' ran memorial articles on Ross.<ref name="NAMS 2003"/><ref name="MAA FOCUS 2003"/><ref name="MAA FOCUS 2002"/> Mathematicians such as [[Karl Rubin]] expressed their personal debts to Ross.<ref name="NAMS 2003"/> He did not have any children.<ref name="NAMS 1996"/><ref name="OSU obituary"/>

== Legacy ==

Ross's biggest contribution to his field was not through his research, but through his mathematics education programs.<ref name="MAA FOCUS 2003"/> He had run each of his summer programs from 1957 to 2000,<ref name="MAA FOCUS 2003"/> working with over 2,000 students.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> His summer program graduates found roles in prestigious research positions in fields across the sciences.<ref name="MAA FOCUS 2003"/> The Ross Program was acclaimed by mathematicians as highly influential.<ref name="Wissner-Gross 2007"/><ref name="MAA FOCUS 2003"/><ref name=Zassenhaus/>

The Ross Program inspired many similar programs, the closest in likeness being the Program in Mathematics for Young Scientists (PROMYS) at [[Boston University]] and the Honors Math Camp at [[Southwest Texas State University]].<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Other programs at [[University of Chicago]] and [[University of Texas at San Antonio]] were inspired by Ross.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> The founders of PROMYS were Ross Program alumni,<ref name="Wissner-Gross 2007"/> and when the Ross Program went to the University of Chicago for several years, mathematics chair [[Paul Sally]] slowly became supportive of the program and later began his own gifted students program.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Informally, Ross Program and Ross's students are known as "Ross-1s" and those who study under them (including PROMYS attendees) are known as "Ross-2s".<ref name="Wissner-Gross 2007"/>

The Arnold Ross Lecture Series founded in his name in 1993<ref name="OSU obituary"/> and run by the [[American Mathematical Society]] puts mathematicians before high school audiences annually in cities across the United States.<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> Ohio State University organized two reunion-conferences for Ross with program alumni, friends of Ross, and a series of science lectures,<ref name="NAMS 2001"/> in 1996 and 2001.<ref name="OSU 2002"/>
